analysis.one_liner: Repeals the tax and fee increases Congress passed in the 1990 budget deal.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 7 House Republicans, was referred to two committees and a subcommittee and never advanced before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The 1990 budget agreement raised money to cut the deficit through higher income tax rates on upper incomes, new luxury taxes on yachts, cars, jewelry, furs, and aircraft, and higher excise taxes and user fees on things like gasoline, alcohol, and tobacco. This bill would wipe out all of those increases, restoring the tax law to what it was before the 1990 deal. It went nowhere in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households would pay less income tax, since the 1990 law raised their rates and layered on a 3% surcharge; wealthy buyers of boats, expensive cars, jewelry, furs, and aircraft would no longer pay the new luxury taxes; and drivers, drinkers, and smokers would pay lower federal excise taxes. Luxury-goods industries and their suppliers would regain customers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, luxury-goods buyers and makers

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals titles X and XI of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1990 and applies the law as if those titles had never been enacted [S3].
Those titles contained the 1990 budget act's specified fee and tax increases, which the Congressional Research Service identifies as the bill's target [S2].
For ordinary consumers, repeal would mean lower federal taxes at the pump and on alcohol and tobacco products, which were raised in the 1990 budget deal.

analysis.who_pays: The lost revenue — the 1990 taxes were enacted specifically to reduce the federal deficit — would be added back to the deficit or have to be made up elsewhere, unless other spending or taxes were cut. Federal programs funded through those fees and taxes would lose that money.

drawbacks.text: The 1990 tax increases were the revenue side of a deficit-reduction package; repealing them would undo that deficit reduction and add to federal borrowing, a cost that eventually falls on all taxpayers [S2].

The relief is tilted upward: the income tax and luxury tax changes primarily benefit high-income households and wealthy buyers, while the excise tax relief for ordinary consumers is modest per household.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ordinary consumers would get small, real savings on gasoline, alcohol, and tobacco taxes, but the largest benefits flow to high-income households and luxury-goods buyers, and the bill offers no replacement for the revenue, so the deficit — a cost borne broadly — would grow. On balance, the bill serves concentrated interests more than the general public.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means and Government Operations committees and then to a subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John J. Rhodes III introduced the bill on March 31, 1992, and it was referred jointly to the House Committees on Ways and Means and Government Operations [S5].
Six House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].

On April 3, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Legislation and National Security, and the action history shows no markup, no floor vote, and no further action for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The 1990 budget deal's tax increases stayed in place, preserving the revenue meant for deficit reduction. High earners, luxury-goods buyers, and the industries behind them did not get the repeal they sought.

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters — the sponsor and six cosponsors — were Republicans; the bill was referred to committees controlled by the Democratic majority and never advanced.

industries.industry: Luxury goods (yacht and boat builders, jewelry, furs, aircraft, luxury cars)
industries.note: The 1990 law imposed a 10% excise tax on luxury goods; repeal would remove it. The best-known argument for repeal came from boat builders whose sales and jobs collapsed after the tax, so the industry's interest here ran partly alongside its workers'.

Repeal would remove the higher income tax rates and the 3% surcharge on upper incomes enacted in 1990. That relief would come at the cost of the revenue meant for deficit reduction, which benefits the public broadly.
The 1990 law raised federal excise taxes on alcohol and tobacco; repeal would lower them, modestly cutting prices for consumers and lifting sales for producers.
The 1990 law added 2.5 cents per gallon to the federal gasoline tax; repeal would remove it. Drivers would save a little at the pump; producers and retailers sell the same fuel either way.
